questions.question: Utility is described as SUBJECTIVE because:
options: It exists in the person using the good, so it varies between people, places and moments
It is impossible to experience
It is fixed by the manufacturer
It always equals the price

questions.question: Water's VALUE IN USE is immense, yet its VALUE IN EXCHANGE is tiny. The resolution of this paradox is:
options: Water is actually useless
Exchange value runs on scarcity and the utility of the NEXT unit, not total usefulness
Diamonds are more useful than water
Governments keep water cheap by law everywhere

questions.question: Trade is possible at all because:
options: Everyone values everything equally
Sellers always overprice
The same thing carries different worth for different people — worth more to the buyer than to the seller
Money forces people to exchange

questions.question: PRICE is best defined as:
options: Value in use expressed in words
The cost of production only
A number chosen by the seller's feelings
Value in exchange expressed in money — one shared language for all exchange values

questions.question: Which set lists conditions of a PERFECT market?
options: Many buyers and sellers, homogeneous product, perfect knowledge, free entry and exit
One seller, unique product, secret prices, blocked entry
Few sellers, branded products, loyalty programmes
Government-set prices and licensed sellers only

questions.question: Under perfect competition every participant is a PRICE TAKER because:
options: The law forbids bargaining
No single buyer or seller is large enough to sway the price — the market's crossing point sets it for everyone
Sellers agree on prices in advance
Prices never change in perfect markets

questions.question: A handful of big banks pricing fees with one eye on each other is an example of:
options: Perfect competition
Monopoly
Oligopoly — a few large sellers watching one another
Monopolistic competition

questions.question: Coffee shops that differ by roast, decor and location, each with slight pricing power, illustrate:
options: Monopoly
Perfect competition
Oligopoly
Monopolistic competition — many sellers of similar but differentiated products

subtopics.title: World Markets and the Effects of Electronics

questions.question: The gold price matters to South African mining towns because:
options: It is set by global world-market trading, yet decides local incomes and jobs
Local mines set the world price
Gold is only sold inside South Africa
The price never changes

questions.question: A livestock farmer checking auction prices in a group chat before the buyer arrives illustrates electronics improving:
options: Free exit from the market
KNOWLEDGE — the perfect-market condition moving from fiction toward daily fact
Product homogeneity
Government regulation

questions.question: A home baker entering the cake market through a social-media page, without premises, shows electronics:
options: Raising barriers to entry
Slowing markets down
Lowering entry barriers — joining a market without a shopfront
Eliminating competition

questions.question: The balanced view of electronic markets includes which caution?
options: Phones make all markets perfectly fair
Electronic trade has no downsides
Only cash markets can be trusted
Platform owners hold gate power, small sellers face global rivals, and the digital divide is a new barrier to entry

questions.question: The five functions of markets are:
options: Price formation, allocation, information, rationing, linking buyers and sellers
Taxing, spending, saving, borrowing, lending
Producing, packaging, advertising, delivering, recycling
Importing, exporting, storing, insuring, auditing

questions.question: A rising price drawing labour and capital toward a product demonstrates:
options: The rationing function failing
ALLOCATION — prices steering resources toward what society wants more of
The information function breaking down
Perfect knowledge

questions.question: Calling a price "a compressed message" refers to:
options: Prices being printed in small font
Sellers hiding information from buyers
The INFORMATION function — one number carrying news of scarcity, costs and tastes to millions at once
Advertising slogans

questions.question: The honest footnote attached to the five functions is:
options: Markets always serve everyone equally
Markets never perform their functions
The functions only work in rich countries
Markets serve buying power — where need has no income behind it, the state's corrections are called in

subtopics.title: Why Water Costs R30 at the Festival

questions.question: The same bottle costs R9 at the café and R30 inside the festival because:
options: The buyer changed — hot, thirsty and fenced in, the utility of that bottle soared
The water inside the fence is of higher quality
The festival pays higher water taxes
The café sells at a loss

questions.question: In the water-diamond riddle, diamonds win on trading-worth because:
options: Diamonds keep people alive
Scarcity — one more diamond is a prize, while one more glass of water to someone with plenty is nearly worthless
Water cannot be traded at all
Diamonds have more value in use

questions.question: The festival fence "proves the rule in reverse" because:
options: Fences reduce all prices
Utility disappears inside fences
Fencing the crowd in makes water inside scarce — and its trading-worth more than triples
The rule only applies to diamonds

subtopics.title: The Tomato Market and the Big Four Banks

questions.question: The sunrise tomato market approaches a PERFECT market because:
options: Identical crates, many growers and buyers, visible prices, and anyone may pitch up tomorrow
One grower sets the price for all
Tomatoes are branded and differentiated
Entry requires an expensive licence

questions.question: The patented drought-resistant seed with no substitute is a monopoly, so its holder is:
options: A price taker like everyone else
A price MAKER — choosing the price, limited only by what buyers can bear
Forced to charge the tomato-market price
Barred from selling to farmers

questions.question: Asking double at the tomato market simply loses you customers because:
options: Tomatoes cannot legally cost more
Buyers dislike bargaining
Everyone TAKES the market price — buyers step to the next identical stall
The market manager fines overchargers

questions.question: The three street-level sorting questions for any market are:
options: Who is richest, who is oldest, who arrived first?
What is taxed, what is imported, what is advertised?
Is it indoors, is it outdoors, is it online?
How many sellers; identical or differentiated product; how easily can a newcomer enter?

questions.question: The farmer scrolling auction prices before the buyer's bakkie arrives gains:
options: Bargaining power — negotiating from knowledge of the going price
Nothing; gate prices are fixed
A legal obligation to sell
Higher transport costs

questions.question: "The phone dragged perfect knowledge halfway into daily life" means:
options: Phones know everything perfectly
A once-fictional textbook condition — everyone informed about prices — is now partly real for anyone with data
Textbooks are no longer needed
Prices stopped changing

questions.question: The economist's audit of the pocket market warns that:
options: Online selling is always unprofitable
Electronic markets have abolished scarcity
Platform owners guard the gates, local sellers face distant rivals, and those without data stand locked outside
Cash will disappear next year

questions.question: "Markets make prices, and prices do the rest" summarises:
options: Prices replacing money
Markets working only when supervised
Sellers controlling all five functions
The five functions — formation first, then allocation, information, rationing and connection all flowing from the price
